newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus in crisis on last day of referendum poll.
newsitem.headline: Belarus in crisis on last day of referendum poll.

text.p: Belarus was gripped by political crisis as it entered the last day of a referendum vote on Sunday with hardline President Alexander Lukashenko bidding to widen his powers and extend his term of office.

The former Soviet republic plunged back into crisis on Saturday when Lukashenko and a rebellious parliament both reneged on a deal brokered by neighbouring Russia aimed at resolving their dispute over the referendum.

A defiant Lukashenko addressed the nation of 10 million people on state television on Saturday, pointing to religious and ethnic conflicts in other former Soviet republics and saying the country he runs is an island of stability.
Lukashenko, 42, wants to use the referendum to tighten his grip on rival institutions, including parliament, and extend his term by more than two years -- an idea parliamentarians oppose.
"It is not a choice between president and parliament. It is a choice between chaos and anarchy on one hand, and discipline, order and a changes for the better on the other," he said.

He declared that only his draft constitution would bring stability, saying: "Look at the situation in the other former Soviet republics, the religious and ethnic conflicts. Only our country is an island of stability in this chaos and anarchy."

Communists, liberals and nationalists have recently joined forces to oppose Lukashenko and his authoritarian style of rule. But there is a lack of strong opposition leadership in this nation sandwiched between Russia and Poland.
Voting began in November 9 in the referendum, with seven questions to be answered including one on whether to accept Lukashenko's draft constitution on extending his powers.
Each side blamed the other for the collapse of the agreement, which deputies failed to pass on Friday.
Lukashenko compared deputies to animals in a zoo and said he had cancelled his half of the accord brokered by Russia after parliament had failed to approve it.
Moscow is Lukashenko's closest ally and the Kremlin is seen as the only power with enough clout to influence him.
Russia's ORT television, which tends to back the Kremlin, broadcast an anti-Lukashenko item late on Saturday and a long interview with his main foe, parliament chief Semyon Sharetsky.
Lukashenko's voice was heard praising Hitler for bringing order to pre-war Germany and footage of a concentration camp was shown.
The foreign ministry sent a protest to the Russian ministry over the item on the "Vremya" programme, saying Lukashenko's voice had been faked, the television said.
Lukashenko on Saturday said he would ensure Sunday's vote was mandatory, contradicting the deal mediated by Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.

Sharetsky, who signed the agreement, said: "The situation in Belarus is getting worse and tensions are growing. We thought we would be able to calm the storm. But the president wanted and still wants to grab more power by anti-constitutional means."

Lukashenko said parliament's failure to pass the deal showed disrespect to everyone involved, including Russia, which hailed the accord as a great success for its diplomacy and for the "community" it formed with Belarus last April.
Lukashenko recalled his visit to parliament, where debates raged all day on Friday and one of his supporters tried to grab the microphone after another deputy called Lukashenko a tyrant.
"Excuse me, but it was like a menagerie," he told a television interviewer. "Three at the back shouting, another one shouting on the left, another one jumping, someone hollering, someone whistling."

It was not clear if Lukashenko had consulted Russia, guarantor of the accord, before deciding to cancel the deal but Moscow's ambassador described the situation as "very bad" and said Russia might intervene again to try to solve the crisis.
Yeltsin's spokesman said on Saturday the president considered Friday's compromise as the first key step in ending the conflict, despite its apparent failure.

The constitutional court in Minsk put off until Tuesday a decision on a bid by deputies to remove Lukashenko from office by impeachment. A deputy who attended the court session said earlier that one judge was absent and the court was split 5-5.
